title: Chapter 12 summary and quiz
recap: An optional result can describe a mutation that may fail, while pointers identify optional caller-owned objects. Treat validation as a transaction boundary: do not change state until every precondition passes.
Aliasing matters when multiple parameters identify writable objects. Explicitly rejecting identical accounts makes the contract predictable and keeps validation independent of mutation order.
objectives: Implement the stated behavior for multiple inputs.
Run the visible tests and explain one boundary case.
warnings: The function/type interface is fixed, but implementation syntax is your choice.
Do not remove the visible tests; the checker keeps an independent copy.
Respect the stated input domain and lifetime/range rules.
challenge: Implement transfer(from,to,amount), returning optional<int> with the new source balance on success. Both pointers must be non-null and distinct, both balances nonnegative, amount nonnegative, and source must have enough funds. On any invalid condition return nullopt and change neither balance. A zero transfer succeeds. Starting balances and amount are at most 10000, so sums fit int. Do not allocate or own the pointed-to accounts.
expectedOutput: amount greater than balance -> nullopt, unchanged
hints: Validate null and identical pointers before dereferencing.
Validate balances and amount before changing either balance.
Return the new source balance, including an engaged optional containing zero.
